claim: GLI1 expression in the synovial tissue of RA patients was positively correlated with RA-related scores.
source: GLI1 expression in the synovial tissue of RA patients was positively correlated with RA-related scores and was highly expressed in collagen-induced arthritis (CIA) mouse articular macrophage-like cells.
evidence: The manuscript states a correlation between GLI1 expression and RA-related scores based on patient data analysis.

claim: GLI1 was highly expressed in collagen-induced arthritis (CIA) mouse articular macrophage-like cells.
source: GLI1 expression in the synovial tissue of RA patients was positively correlated with RA-related scores and was highly expressed in collagen-induced arthritis (CIA) mouse articular macrophage-like cells.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental observation of GLI1 expression in CIA mouse cells.

claim: Decreased expression and inhibition of nuclear transfer of GLI1 downregulated macrophage M1 polarization.
source: The decreased expression and inhibition of nuclear transfer of GLI1 downregulated macrophage M1 polarization and osteoclast activation, the effect of which was achieved by modulation of DNA methyltransferases (DNMTs) via transcriptional regulation and protein interactions.
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental results showing the effect of GLI1 inhibition on M1 polarization.

claim: Decreased expression and inhibition of nuclear transfer of GLI1 downregulated osteoclast activation.
source: The decreased expression and inhibition of nuclear transfer of GLI1 downregulated macrophage M1 polarization and osteoclast activation, the effect of which was achieved by modulation of DNA methyltransferases (DNMTs) via transcriptional regulation and protein interactions.
evidence: The manuscript describes experimental results showing the effect of GLI1 inhibition on osteoclast activation.

claim: The effect of GLI1 on macrophage M1 polarization and osteoclast activation was achieved by modulation of DNA methyltransferases (DNMTs) via transcriptional regulation and protein interactions.
source: The decreased expression and inhibition of nuclear transfer of GLI1 downregulated macrophage M1 polarization and osteoclast activation, the effect of which was achieved by modulation of DNA methyltransferases (DNMTs) via transcriptional regulation and protein interactions.
evidence: The manuscript presents mechanistic data showing GLI1 regulates DNMTs through transcriptional and protein interaction mechanisms.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of GLI1 significantly reduced the proportion of proinflammatory macrophages in CIA mice.
source: By pharmacological inhibition of GLI1, the proportion of proinflammatory macrophages and the number of osteoclasts were significantly reduced, and the joint inflammatory response and bone destruction in CIA mice were alleviated.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results from in vivo studies using GLI1 inhibitor.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of GLI1 significantly reduced the number of osteoclasts in CIA mice.
source: By pharmacological inhibition of GLI1, the proportion of proinflammatory macrophages and the number of osteoclasts were significantly reduced, and the joint inflammatory response and bone destruction in CIA mice were alleviated.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results from in vivo studies using GLI1 inhibitor.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of GLI1 alleviated joint inflammatory response in CIA mice.
source: By pharmacological inhibition of GLI1, the proportion of proinflammatory macrophages and the number of osteoclasts were significantly reduced, and the joint inflammatory response and bone destruction in CIA mice were alleviated.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results from in vivo studies using GLI1 inhibitor.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of GLI1 alleviated bone destruction in CIA mice.
source: By pharmacological inhibition of GLI1, the proportion of proinflammatory macrophages and the number of osteoclasts were significantly reduced, and the joint inflammatory response and bone destruction in CIA mice were alleviated.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results from in vivo studies using GLI1 inhibitor.

claim: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is characterized by joint synovitis and bone destruction.
source: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is characterized by joint synovitis and bone destruction, the etiology of which remains to be explored.
evidence: This is a well-established characteristic of RA in the medical literature.

claim: The etiology of rheumatoid arthritis remains to be explored.
source: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is characterized by joint synovitis and bone destruction, the etiology of which remains to be explored.
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges the incomplete understanding of RA etiology.

claim: Overactivation of M1 macrophages has been thought to be an essential cause of joint inflammation in RA.
source: Many types of cells are involved in the progression of RA joint inflammation, among which the overactivation of M1 macrophages and osteoclasts has been thought to be an essential cause of joint inflammation and bone destruction.
evidence: This is supported by citations and established knowledge in the field.

claim: Overactivation of osteoclasts has been thought to be an essential cause of bone destruction in RA.
source: Many types of cells are involved in the progression of RA joint inflammation, among which the overactivation of M1 macrophages and osteoclasts has been thought to be an essential cause of joint inflammation and bone destruction.
evidence: This is supported by citations and established knowledge in the field.

claim: Glioma-associated oncogene homolog 1 (GLI1) has been revealed to be closely linked to bone metabolism.
source: Glioma-associated oncogene homolog 1 (GLI1) has been revealed to be closely linked to bone metabolism.
evidence: This statement is based on prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: RA currently affects approximately 75 million people worldwide.
source: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a common chronic inflammatory disease that currently affects approximately 75 million people worldwide.
evidence: This is a statistical claim supported by citation (Kim et al., 2019).

claim: RA can eventually lead to disability or even death.
source: In addition to arthritis symptoms, RA can eventually lead to disability or even death (Firestein, 2003; Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Synovial inflammation and bone erosion are the direct factors causing joint damage in RA.
source: Although the mechanism of RA is not clear, it is generally believed that synovial inflammation and bone erosion are the direct factors causing joint damage.
evidence: This is a generally accepted understanding in the field.

claim: Persistent activation of immune cells leads to the progression of symptoms such as synovitis in RA.
source: Persistent activation of immune cells leads to the progression of symptoms such as synovitis in RA.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RA pathophysiology.

claim: RA is an immune-mediated disorder involving both innate and adaptive cellular compartments.
source: This immune-mediated disorder involves both innate and adaptive cellular compartments as well as their dysregulated cytokine production.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RA pathophysiology.

claim: The pathological process of RA is promoted through the synergistic action of osteoclasts, chondrocytes and stromal cells.
source: In addition, the pathological process of RA is promoted through the synergistic action of the cellular resident in the bone and in joint compartments, such as osteoclasts, chondrocytes and stromal cells (Komatsu and Takayanagi, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Komatsu and Takayanagi, 2022.

claim: Macrophages have a key role in the innate immune function that causes inflammation in RA.
source: Within the innate immune function that causes inflammation, macrophages have a key role.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Macrophages contribute to normal tissue homeostasis, working as antigen-presenting cells (APCs) to activate adaptive immunity, pathogen expulsion, resolution of inflammation and wound healing.
source: In fact, they contribute to normal tissue homeostasis, working as antigen-presenting cells (APCs) to activate adaptive immunity, pathogen expulsion, resolution of inflammation and wound healing (Tardito et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tardito et al., 2019.

claim: Classically activated macrophages (M1) have been proven to be dominant in RA joints.
source: Classically activated macrophages (M1), which have been proven to be dominant in RA joints, cause joint erosion, secreting principally proinflammatory cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor α (TNF-α), interleukin 1β (IL-1β) and IL-6, whereas alternatively activated macrophages (M2) contribute to tissue remodeling and repair via high production of anti-inflammatory cytokines (mainly IL-10 and TGF-β) (Cho et al., 2014; Tardito et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: M1 macrophages cause joint erosion by secreting principally proinflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α, IL-1β and IL-6.
source: Classically activated macrophages (M1), which have been proven to be dominant in RA joints, cause joint erosion, secreting principally proinflammatory cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor α (TNF-α), interleukin 1β (IL-1β) and IL-6, whereas alternatively activated macrophages (M2) contribute to tissue remodeling and repair via high production of anti-inflammatory cytokines (mainly IL-10 and TGF-β) (Cho et al., 2014; Tardito et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: M2 macrophages contribute to tissue remodeling and repair via high production of anti-inflammatory cytokines (mainly IL-10 and TGF-β).
source: Classically activated macrophages (M1), which have been proven to be dominant in RA joints, cause joint erosion, secreting principally proinflammatory cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor α (TNF-α), interleukin 1β (IL-1β) and IL-6, whereas alternatively activated macrophages (M2) contribute to tissue remodeling and repair via high production of anti-inflammatory cytokines (mainly IL-10 and TGF-β) (Cho et al., 2014; Tardito et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Irreversible bone destruction in RA is led by osteoclasts.
source: Another hallmark is irreversible bone destruction, which is led by osteoclasts.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The RA microenvironment and proinflammatory cytokines stimulate the formation of osteoclasts.
source: The RA microenvironment and proinflammatory cytokines stimulate the formation of osteoclasts, which have long been considered the only cells capable of absorbing bone matrix, and the subsequent degradation of bone and cartilage (Bustamante et al., 2017; Woo et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Osteoclasts have long been considered the only cells capable of absorbing bone matrix.
source: The RA microenvironment and proinflammatory cytokines stimulate the formation of osteoclasts, which have long been considered the only cells capable of absorbing bone matrix, and the subsequent degradation of bone and cartilage (Bustamante et al., 2017; Woo et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The hedgehog pathway has been shown to be closely involved in osteogenesis.
source: The hedgehog pathway, which has been shown to be closely involved in osteogenesis (Jemtland et al., 2003), is highly conserved and critical for normal embryogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jemtland et al., 2003.

claim: The hedgehog pathway is highly conserved and critical for normal embryogenesis.
source: The hedgehog pathway, which has been shown to be closely involved in osteogenesis (Jemtland et al., 2003), is highly conserved and critical for normal embryogenesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge in developmental biology.

claim: The hedgehog protein family consists of hedgehog ligands that bind the cell surface transmembrane receptor patch (PTCH) and function through posttranslational processing of glioma-associated oncogene homolog (GLI) zinc finger transcription factors.
source: The hedgehog protein family consists of hedgehog ligands that bind the cell surface transmembrane receptor patch (PTCH) and function through posttranslational processing of glioma-associated oncogene homolog (GLI) zinc finger transcription factors (Rimkus et al., 2016; Sasai et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rimkus et al., 2016 and Sasai et al., 2019.

claim: Three mammalian GLI proteins have been identified.
source: To date, three mammalian GLI proteins have been identified, among which GLI1 usually acts as a transcriptional activator.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: GLI1 usually acts as a transcriptional activator.
source: To date, three mammalian GLI proteins have been identified, among which GLI1 usually acts as a transcriptional activator.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: GANT58 is a selective inhibitor of GLI1.
source: On the basis of these studies, small molecular compounds such as GANT58 (selective inhibitor of GLI1) and GANT61 (inhibitor of GLI1 and GLI2) are often used as pharmacological interventions of GLI1, so as to achieve the purpose of inhibiting GLI1 activity and regulating the molecular biological processes (Chen et al., 2018; Schneider et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2018 and Schneider et al., 2018.

claim: GANT61 is an inhibitor of GLI1 and GLI2.
source: On the basis of these studies, small molecular compounds such as GANT58 (selective inhibitor of GLI1) and GANT61 (inhibitor of GLI1 and GLI2) are often used as pharmacological interventions of GLI1, so as to achieve the purpose of inhibiting GLI1 activity and regulating the molecular biological processes (Chen et al., 2018; Schneider et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2018 and Schneider et al., 2018.

claim: GLI1-activated transcription promotes the development of inflammatory diseases such as gastritis.
source: Relevant studies have shown that GLI1-activated transcription promotes the development of inflammatory diseases such as gastritis, and antagonizing GLI1 transcription can alleviate the inflammatory degradation of articular cartilage (Ali et al., 2016; Kopinke et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ali et al., 2016 and Kopinke et al., 2021.

claim: Antagonizing GLI1 transcription can alleviate the inflammatory degradation of articular cartilage.
source: Relevant studies have shown that GLI1-activated transcription promotes the development of inflammatory diseases such as gastritis, and antagonizing GLI1 transcription can alleviate the inflammatory degradation of articular cartilage (Ali et al., 2016; Kopinke et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ali et al., 2016 and Kopinke et al., 2021.

claim: DNA methylation is activated by DNA methyltransferases (DNMTs).
source: DNA methylation, which is activated by DNA methyltransferases (DNMTs), is an important epigenetic marker that plays an important role in regulating gene expression, maintaining chromatin structure, gene imprinting, X chromosome inactivation and embryo development (Li and Zhang, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li and Zhang, 2014.

claim: DNA methylation is an important epigenetic marker that plays an important role in regulating gene expression, maintaining chromatin structure, gene imprinting, X chromosome inactivation and embryo development.
source: DNA methylation, which is activated by DNA methyltransferases (DNMTs), is an important epigenetic marker that plays an important role in regulating gene expression, maintaining chromatin structure, gene imprinting, X chromosome inactivation and embryo development (Li and Zhang, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li and Zhang, 2014.

claim: DNMT1 and DNMT3a are involved in the progression of many physiological disorders, such as the immune response and cell differentiation.
source: As reported, DNMT1 and DNMT3a are involved in the progression of many physiological disorders, such as the immune response and cell differentiation (Fu et al., 2022; Ramabadran et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fu et al., 2022 and Ramabadran et al., 2023.

claim: Compared with normal synovial tissue, the synovium of RA patients had a high degree of inflammatory cell infiltration.
source: Compared with normal synovial tissue, the synovium of RA patients had a high degree of inflammatory cell infiltration (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is based on histological analysis shown in Figure 1A.

claim: There were more GLI1-positive cells in RA synovium than in normal synovium.
source: Immunohistochemical (IHC) staining showed that there were more GLI1-positive cells in RA synovium than in normal synovium (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is based on IHC staining results shown in Figures 1B and C.

claim: Western blotting verified the upregulation of GLI1 in the joint synovium of RA patients.
source: The results of western blotting further verified the upregulation of GLI1 in the joint synovium of RA patients (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is based on western blotting results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: GLI1 was more highly expressed in RA patients with higher DAS28 scores.
source: We performed a DAS28 score on the included patients to initially assess RA activity and then matched the relative expression of GLI1 with them, indicating that GLI1 was more highly expressed in RA patients.
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis between DAS28 scores and GLI1 expression.

claim: All mice in the CIA model survived and were included in the analysis.
source: All mice survived and were included in the analysis.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental outcome.

claim: H&E staining results showed no hepatorenal toxicity of GANT58.
source: H&E staining results showed no hepatorenal toxicity of GANT58 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on histological analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: After secondary immunization, CIA mouse paws swelled rapidly.
source: After secondary immunization, CIA mouse paws swelled rapidly, and weight loss occurred simultaneously, which could be reversed by GANT58 treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A, B).
evidence: This is based on observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A, B.

claim: Weight loss occurred in CIA mice after secondary immunization.
source: After secondary immunization, CIA mouse paws swelled rapidly, and weight loss occurred simultaneously, which could be reversed by GANT58 treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A, B).
evidence: This is based on observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A, B.

claim: GANT58 treatment reversed paw swelling and weight loss in CIA mice.
source: After secondary immunization, CIA mouse paws swelled rapidly, and weight loss occurred simultaneously, which could be reversed by GANT58 treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A, B).
evidence: This is based on observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A, B.

claim: After 21 days of modeling, the arthritis scores of mice in the vehicle group increased significantly.
source: Based on the arthritis score, it could be observed that after 21 days of modeling, the scores of the mice in the vehicle group increased significantly.
evidence: This is based on arthritis scoring data.

claim: The arthritis scores of GANT58-treated mice were remarkably lower than those of mice in the vehicle group.
source: Obviously, the arthritis scores of GANT58-treated mice were remarkably lower than those of mice in the vehicle group (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on arthritis scoring data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: CIA mice had obvious signs of arthritis in their hind paws.
source: We photographed the hind paws of mice in each group and found that CIA mice had obvious signs of arthritis, while mice in the GANT58 treatment group showed a slight degree of swelling, which was similar to that of normal mice (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is based on photographic evidence shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Mice in the GANT58 treatment group showed a slight degree of swelling, which was similar to that of normal mice.
source: We photographed the hind paws of mice in each group and found that CIA mice had obvious signs of arthritis, while mice in the GANT58 treatment group showed a slight degree of swelling, which was similar to that of normal mice (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is based on photographic evidence shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Vehicle group mice had more obvious bone destruction compared with sham group mice.
source: As shown in Figure 1F, compared with sham group mice, vehicle group mice had more obvious bone destruction, and GANT58 treatment alleviated this effect.
evidence: This is based on Micro-CT imaging shown in Figure 1F.

claim: GANT58 treatment alleviated bone destruction in CIA mice.
source: As shown in Figure 1F, compared with sham group mice, vehicle group mice had more obvious bone destruction, and GANT58 treatment alleviated this effect.
evidence: This is based on Micro-CT imaging shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Bone parameters were markedly better in the GANT58-treated mice than in the vehicle control mice.
source: Through the analysis of bone parameters in the joint part of the mouse foot claw, we also found that the bone parameters were markedly better in the GANT58-treated mice than in the vehicle control mice (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is based on bone parameter analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: GANT58 intervention significantly reduced the degree of inflammatory cell infiltration in mouse joints.
source: The results showed that GANT58 intervention significantly reduced the degree of inflammatory cell infiltration and joint bone destruction (Figure 1H, I, Figure 1—figure supplement 3C, D).
evidence: This is based on histological analysis shown in Figures 1H, I, and Figure 1—figure supplement 3C, D.

claim: GANT58 intervention significantly reduced joint bone destruction in CIA mice.
source: The results showed that GANT58 intervention significantly reduced the degree of inflammatory cell infiltration and joint bone destruction (Figure 1H, I, Figure 1—figure supplement 3C, D).
evidence: This is based on histological analysis shown in Figures 1H, I, and Figure 1—figure supplement 3C, D.

claim: The high expression of GLI1 in CIA mice was mostly located in macrophage-like cells.
source: Thus, we performed immunofluorescence colocalization staining of the macrophage marker F4/80 and GLI1 both in subchondral bone marrow cavity and synovial tissue and observed that the high expression of GLI1 in CIA mice was mostly located in macrophage-like cells (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence colocalization staining shown in Figure 1J.

claim: GLI1 protein expression increased at 24 hr after LPS and IFN-γ induction.
source: To investigate the relationship between GLI1 expression and M1 macrophages in vitro, we first measured GLI1 protein expression by western blotting during M1 macrophage induction, which increased at 24 hr after LPS and IFN-γ induction (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is based on western blotting results shown in Figures 2A and B.

claim: After LPS/IFN-γ intervention, the expression of GLI1 in the nucleus increased.
source: As shown in Figure 2A, after LPS/IFN-γ intervention, although the amount within the cytoplasm did not change significantly, the expression of GLI1 in the nucleus increased to certain degrees, suggesting that GLI1 was activated and incorporated into the nucleus during the M1 polarization process to play a related regulatory role.
evidence: This is based on western blotting of nuclear and cytoplasmic fractions shown in Figure 2A.

claim: GLI1 was activated and incorporated into the nucleus during the M1 polarization process.
source: As shown in Figure 2A, after LPS/IFN-γ intervention, although the amount within the cytoplasm did not change significantly, the expression of GLI1 in the nucleus increased to certain degrees, suggesting that GLI1 was activated and incorporated into the nucleus during the M1 polarization process to play a related regulatory role.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of increased nuclear GLI1 expression.

claim: GANT58 had no significant inhibitory effect on BMMs or RAW264.7 cells until the concentration reached 40 μM.
source: Cell viability was measured by CCK-8 assay before the in vitro use of GANT58, and the results showed that GANT58 had no significant inhibitory effect on either BMMs or RAW264.7 cells until the concentration reached 40 μM (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This is based on CCK-8 assay results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: GANT58 at a concentration of 10 μM reduced the expression of GLI1.
source: We treated cells with a concentration of 10 μM and found that it reduced the expression of GLI1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This is based on experimental results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, B.

claim: After the inhibitory intervention of GLI1, the content of IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α was significantly reduced.
source: Stimulated by LPS and IFN-γ, macrophages release a large number of proinflammatory cytokines, including IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α. After the inhibitory intervention of GLI1, the content of these cytokines was significantly reduced, while the release inhibition of IL-10 was alleviated to some extent (Figure 2C–F).
evidence: This is based on ELISA results shown in Figures 2C–F.

claim: After the inhibitory intervention of GLI1, the release inhibition of IL-10 was alleviated to some extent.
source: Stimulated by LPS and IFN-γ, macrophages release a large number of proinflammatory cytokines, including IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α. After the inhibitory intervention of GLI1, the content of these cytokines was significantly reduced, while the release inhibition of IL-10 was alleviated to some extent (Figure 2C–F).
evidence: This is based on ELISA results shown in Figures 2C–F.

claim: The GANT58 group exhibited fewer iNOS-positive cells compared to cells in the LPS and IFN-γ-treated groups.
source: Immunofluorescence staining suggested that the GANT58 group exhibited fewer iNOS-positive cells and near-basic levels of Arg-1 expression compared to cells in the LPS and IFN-γ-treated groups (Figure 2G–I), and the western blot results supported the same conclusion (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A, B).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence staining shown in Figures 2G–I.

claim: The GANT58 group exhibited near-basic levels of Arg-1 expression compared to cells in the LPS and IFN-γ-treated groups.
source: Immunofluorescence staining suggested that the GANT58 group exhibited fewer iNOS-positive cells and near-basic levels of Arg-1 expression compared to cells in the LPS and IFN-γ-treated groups (Figure 2G–I), and the western blot results supported the same conclusion (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A, B).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence staining shown in Figures 2G–I.

claim: GANT58 reduced the expression of the Il1b, Il6 and Tnfa genes.
source: The results showed that GANT58 also reduced the expression of the Il1b, Il6 and Tnfa genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is based on RT-qPCR results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: GANT58 significantly reduced the nucleation transport of GLI1.
source: In addition, we examined the expression and distribution of GLI1 in cells under different interventions and found that GANT58 significantly reduced the nucleation transport of GLI1 while inhibiting the proinflammatory state of cells (Figure 2J and K).
evidence: This is based on western blotting and immunofluorescence results shown in Figures 2J and K.

claim: siGli1 macrophages showed lower iNOS expression induced by LPS and IFN-γ compared with wild-type (WT) macrophages.
source: As shown in Figure 2L and M, compared with wild-type (WT) macrophages, siGli1 macrophages showed lower iNOS expression induced by LPS and IFN-γ.
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence staining shown in Figures 2L and M.

claim: The number of CD86-positive M1 macrophages in the synovial tissue of mice in the CIA model group was higher than after GANT58 treatment.
source: Subsequently, we performed immunofluorescence co-staining of F4/80 and CD86 in animal model tissues, and compared with more CD86-positive M1 macrophages in the synovial tissue of mice in the CIA model group, the number of positive macrophages of the proinflammatory phenotype after GANT58 treatment was significantly reduced (Figure 2N and O).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence co-staining shown in Figures 2N and O.

claim: After RANKL stimulation, more GLI1 was activated and transferred to the nucleus.
source: The results showed that after RANKL stimulation, more GLI1 was activated and transferred to the nucleus (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is based on western blotting results shown in Figures 3A and B.

claim: There was less osteoclast formation in the GANT58-treated group than in the RANKL stimulation group.
source: As a result, there was less osteoclast formation in the GANT58-treated group than in the RANKL stimulation group (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This is based on TRAP staining results shown in Figures 3C and D.

claim: There was no obvious death or apoptosis at a working concentration of 10 μM GANT58.
source: To eliminate the influence of drug-induced apoptosis on osteoclast activation, we carried out live/dead staining and apoptosis detection on BMMs. We found that there was no obvious death or apoptosis at a working concentration of 10 μM. However, when the concentration was increased by four times, more apoptotic cells appeared (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is based on live/dead staining and apoptosis detection shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: When the concentration of GANT58 was increased to 40 μM, more apoptotic cells appeared.
source: To eliminate the influence of drug-induced apoptosis on osteoclast activation, we carried out live/dead staining and apoptosis detection on BMMs. We found that there was no obvious death or apoptosis at a working concentration of 10 μM. However, when the concentration was increased by four times, more apoptotic cells appeared (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is based on live/dead staining and apoptosis detection shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: The number of NFATc1-positive cells decreased significantly after GANT58 treatment.
source: Osteoclast formation is accompanied by high expression of NFATc1. Immunofluorescence staining showed that the number of NFATc1-positive cells decreased significantly after GANT58 treatment (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 3E.

claim: GANT58 intervention greatly reduced the formation of mature osteoclasts in RAW264.7 cells.
source: Tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP) and F-actin staining confirmed that GANT58 intervention greatly reduced the formation of mature osteoclasts as well (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: This is based on TRAP and F-actin staining shown in Figures 3F and G.

claim: GANT58 hindered the activation of GLI1 translocation into the nucleus during osteoclast induction.
source: Then, we extracted the total protein from RAW264.7 cells with different treatments and performed western blot experiments. According to the results, we found that GANT58 hindered the activation of GLI1 translocation into the nucleus (Figure 3H and I).
evidence: This is based on western blotting results shown in Figures 3H and I.

claim: The inhibition of GLI1 expression reduced the formation of osteoclasts.
source: Subsequently, we further induced osteoclasts in WT and Gli1-knockdown macrophages. The results showed that the inhibition of GLI1 expression reduced the formation of osteoclasts, suggesting the specificity of GLI1 in regulating the activation of osteoclasts (Figure 3J and K).
evidence: This is based on TRAP and F-actin staining shown in Figures 3J and K.

claim: Both GANT58 treatment and Gli1 knockdown significantly inhibited the expression of markers related to osteoclast function, including NFATc1, CTSK and MMP9.
source: During osteoclast induction, both GANT58 treatment and Gli1 knockdown significantly inhibited the expression of markers related to osteoclast function, including NFATc1, CTSK and MMP9 (Figure 3L and M).
evidence: This is based on western blotting results shown in Figures 3L and M.

claim: There was more osteoclast formation around the bone tissue in the CIA model group.
source: The results showed that there was more osteoclast formation around the bone tissue in the CIA model group. After GANT58 treatment, the number of osteoclasts decreased, and the trabecular morphology was close to the normal tissue level (Figure 3N and O).
evidence: This is based on TRAP staining shown in Figures 3N and O.

claim: After GANT58 treatment, the number of osteoclasts decreased in CIA mice.
source: The results showed that there was more osteoclast formation around the bone tissue in the CIA model group. After GANT58 treatment, the number of osteoclasts decreased, and the trabecular morphology was close to the normal tissue level (Figure 3N and O).
evidence: This is based on TRAP staining shown in Figures 3N and O.

claim: More genes were downregulated (143) than upregulated (74) in GANT58-treated cells.
source: The seq data showed that more genes were downregulated (143) than upregulated (74) in GANT58-treated cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: GANT58 intervention in GLI1 affected multiple biological processes, including macrophage chemotaxis and macrophage cytokine production.
source: Among these differentially altered genes, we revealed through Gene Ontology (GO) analysis that GANT58 intervention in GLI1 affected multiple biological processes, including macrophage chemotaxis and macrophage cytokine production (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on GO analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Downregulated genes were involved in the development of human diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis.
source: These downregulated genes were involved in the development of human diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis, as well as organismal systems such as osteoclast differentiation (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on KEGG enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Downregulated genes were involved in organismal systems such as osteoclast differentiation.
source: These downregulated genes were involved in the development of human diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis, as well as organismal systems such as osteoclast differentiation (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on KEGG enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The Dnmt3a gene showed a decreasing trend after GANT58 treatment.
source: It is worth noting that among the genes with altered expression, the Dnmt3a gene of the DNA methyltransferase family showed a decreasing trend (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq heat map shown in Figure 4C.

claim: DNMT1 and DNMT3a are the main methylation regulatory enzymes responsible for the de novo methylation and methylation maintenance of DNA in mammals.
source: In mammals, DNMT1 and DNMT3a are the main methylation regulatory enzymes responsible for the de novo methylation and methylation maintenance of DNA.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of epigenetics.

claim: Dnmt3a was clearly inhibited after GANT58 intervention.
source: Thus, through RT‒qPCR validation, we found that Dnmt3a was clearly inhibited after GANT58 intervention, but the expression of Dnmt1 did not appear to change significantly (Figure 4D).
